title: kv: floorplanner allocator and fragmentation-rescue evictor
author: Ava Martinez
description: Context: We continue to see tail latency spikes in multi-tenant workloads caused by KV cache fragmentation and tenant-level slot starvation. Existing evictors are reactive and treat fragmentation as an outcome rather than a first-class signal. This PR introduces two coordinated pieces: a floorplanner allocator that guarantees compact slot placement and reserved floor slots per tenant, and a fragmentation-rescue evictor (async compactor) that performs latency-aware background coalescing and prioritized spillovers. Motivation: Reduce short-term paging and cross-tenant spill cascades that increase end-to-end inference latency under bursty, mixed-sequence workloads. By steering allocations to reduce fragmentation and by having a low-latency-aware background rescuer that smooths spill events, we expect lower p99 generation latency and fewer sudden increases in GPU memory churn. Design summary: 1) Floorplanner allocator (pkg/kv/cache/floorplanner.go) assigns contiguous allocation windows called floors. Floors are sized based on recent allocation histogram (small/medium/large item buckets) and tenant reservation settings. Floors are reusable and compact-aware: when a floor becomes <threshold occupancy it is flagged for reclamation and put into a "reclaim queue" rather than scattered free slots. 2) Fragmentation-rescue evictor (pkg/kv/cache/compactor/async_rescue.go) runs as a background worker with tunable rate limits bound to latency SLOs. It performs three actions: (a) opportunistic coalescing of sparsely populated floors into fewer floors, (b) prioritized spill of low-quality pages (high-fragmentation penalty + low-hit rate), and (c) preemptive soft-evict when a tenant's reserved floor would otherwise drop below minimum. The rescuer uses a scoring function that combines age, hotness, fragmentation penalty, and downstream paging cost. 3) Eviction policy changes (pkg/kv/cache/evictor.go): we augment the existing LRU-ish scorer with a fragmentation multiplier and a page-cost estimator so that objects that would cause many small free regions are deprioritized for retention. 4) Scheduler integration (internal/serving/scheduler/batch_manager.go): the rescuer exposes a budget token to the batch manager to avoid running heavy coalescing during high-continuous-batching pressure. Continuous batching signals (current_batch_depth, avg_wait_ms) are used to throttle rescuer activity to keep generation latency stable. Implementation notes: - The floorplanner exposes a compact API: Allocate(size, tenantID, hints) -> floorID+offset. Hints include expected-seq-len and lifespan. - Reclamation is non-blocking: a reclaim pass atomically moves live entries into a target floor using KV-level move-without-copy whenever possible (swap pointers to backing store) to minimize copying. - The rescuer uses a two-tier backoff: soft backoff tied to CI-configured latency SLOs and hard backoff when eviction pressure exceeds a reactive threshold. - All new code paths include telemetry: floor occupancy gauges, fragment-score histograms, rescue-run duration, move-bytes, and rescue-induced spill counts. Testing & benchmarks: - Unit tests for allocator invariants, scoring comparator, and reclaim queue logic. - Integration tests simulating mixed-tenancy burst patterns with configurable sequence length distributions. - Microbench: tests/bench/kv_cache_frag_bench.go measures p50/p95/p99 token step latency and spill bytes under a 70/20/10 small/medium/large distribution. Results (summary): - Synthetic bench: p99 generation latency reduced by ~18% under 4x bursty workload with 12 tenants, spill bytes reduced by ~25%. - Long-run stability test (48h): rescue worker did ~420 compaction runs, average rescuer CPU 2.1% on a 16-core box, memory moved ~8GB/day on a heavy churn workload. Rollout & safety: - Feature gated behind runtime flag KV_FLOORPLANNER=on and a tenant opt-in. - Default config disabled for existing Dedicated clusters until we validate with canaries. - If rescue causes latency regressions we can disable rescue worker at runtime or lower its budget token; allocator changes are reversible via a migration utility that drains floors. Follow-ups: - Add eviction score calibration service to autotune fragmentation multiplier based on live SLO signals. - Explore kernel-level pinned-memory moves to accelerate reclaim operations on specific GPUs. - Add a dashboard in Redwood Console for per-tenant floor occupancy and rescue activity. Related PRs: ENG-2336 (design doc), followups will land in feature/kv-floorplanner-tuning and perf-canary adjustments.

review_comments: Ravi Kapoor: Can you clarify the cost model used by the page-cost estimator? The current PR text implies a linear cost per page but we should factor in expected downstream tensorization costs.

Ava Martinez (author): The estimator uses a weighted sum: estimated downstream tokenization cost + estimated kernel memcpy cost. I added comments in evictor.go with tunable coefficients and a test that checks monotonic behavior.
Lena Ortiz: The reclaim move looks like it could race with active readers. How are you ensuring correctness without global pauses?

Ava Martinez: Reclaim uses an epoch-based reader-writer handoff (lightweight RC) and an atomic pointer swap for each moved slot; I added a stress test that exercises concurrent reads/writes and verified no data loss.
Maya Singh: CI perf showed a transient regression at p95 on one run; can we add a guard to avoid rescuer runs when batch depth > 64?
Ava Martinez: Good catch — added a throttle that consults batch_manager current_batch_depth; rescuer defers if depth > configured threshold. Re-ran perf and the regression disappears.
